posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
Does anyone know how to preserve gelatin in solution? I need to wash my gelatin before my experiments and if I leave the washed (now gelled) gelatin in the fridge for longer than about a week it grows a mould. This makes planning experiments difficult because washing lasts the good part of an afternoon. 

I have been thinking about sterilizing the gelatin with a UV facial tanner, but I don't know if that damages the gelatin molecules. And I read somewhere that Salicilic acid helps prevent mould, but that it also prevents gelling if too much is added.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
In food science we lower the pH as a preservative. I don't know if it is possible to lower the pH to 4.2 or better 4.0 for storage then raise it back for use. Sodium Benzoate could also work if it did not interfere later.

Outside of preservatives, all mold needs is a single cell to form. Making sure your gelatin is sterile before storing would go a long way toward preserving it. Heating and covering it before storage may be enough to work. 

Pasteurization is another process that might help. I have not had to use it but the concept was explained to me as a certain amount of time and a certain heat is 1 pasteurization unit. For each food product a number is created by experimentation and then any way of achieving that PU is equivalent. I know it is common for beer to be heated and cooled a few times to achieve the required PUs. The temperatures and times are closely held secrets. Just with my experience with the product the temperatures have to be within 140 to 165F. Budweiser heats the entire sealed package and cools it. This could be done in a canning jar.

Purging the head space of the storage with CO2 could also help.

posts.author: holo_cyware
posts.content_md:
Since Martin obtained quite impressive FEG holograms, we can say that freezing the gelatin solution won't hurt it.

Pasteurisation on the other hand may ruin the gelatine structure, since it could need some prolonged heating to fairy high temperatures. It depends on the stuff you intend to kill. The "yeast" in the beer is more heat sensitive than the meat bacterias (some of these need as much as 90 degreees C for hours to kill).

Not to sure about this one. I believe when you heat gelatin, you break the hydrogen bonds between the amino chains. More heat, more bonds broken but you never actually break the chains themselves. I think the same is with freezing, you may break the hydrogen bonds that formed when the gelatin was curing, but I don't think you can take it any smaller then that. Just my cognitive thinking outloud.
